findings: The new evals exercise the rules. 7/7 with-skill responses match expected behavior.

But 6 of 7 also pass with baseline alone. A careful general-purpose subagent — no skill loaded, no memory files, no conversation context — catches the failure modes from general engineering common sense.

Only Eval 7 (dot-diagram requirement) shows the skill changing the verdict, not just the vocabulary. Baseline calls a fix-loop diagram 'optional'; skill makes it mandatory for round-counter loops with caps + escalations.

Implication: the rules I missed in the prompting session are rules a baseline subagent reaches for automatically. I had MORE context (skill loaded, memory entries, system prompt's trust-but-verify) and STILL performed below the baseline. Not a rule-ignorance failure — a rule-erosion-under-pressure failure.

Stacking more rules into creating-skills body therefore does not change behavior under pressure. The right fix is structural: rules must FIRE at the moment of claim, not exist as background. Until that interrupt exists, this skill is teaching, not enforcing.
verdict: PASS on the eval mechanic. FAIL on the underlying assumption that adding rules to skill bodies changes agent behavior under workflow pressure. Step 9 audit is included anyway because (a) the one row that does change verdicts (row 7) is worth the body cost, and (b) the audit itself is the artifact a future interrupt would run against.
